slides.text: You can already create maps and change them. Now you will use them to solve problems: telling a stored zero from a missing key, walking over every entry, counting things, and keeping a set of values you have seen.

Three sessions:

- **Session 1:** checking if a key is there, and `range` over a map
- **Session 2:** counters and sets
- **Session 3:** groups and maps of maps

A lookup of a missing key gives the zero value, so `0` can mean a stored zero or no entry at all. The lookup can also hand back a second answer: whether the key exists.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
value, found = lookup "tea"

found is true   -> key is stored
found is false -> no such key

slides.text: `range` also walks over a map and gives each key with its value. Go visits the entries in a **random order**, and the order changes from run to run. Use it only for results that do not depend on the order, like a sum or a count.

slides.text:
A counter is a map from something to how many times it appeared. A missing key reads as 0, so adding 1 works even the first time.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
for each word in words
    count of word = count of word + 1

slides.text: A set remembers which values exist and nothing else. Use a map whose values are `bool`: a key stored as `true` is in the set, and a missing key reads as `false`, which means it is not.

exercises.title: Count with a map
exercises.guide: Count how many times each value appears.

chunks.guide: A list of votes, some repeated.
Each vote adds 1 to its own count. The first time, the count starts from 0.

notes.text: Creates the key when it is new.

exercises.guide: Use a set to keep each value only once, in its first order.

chunks.guide: A list with repeated names.
The set remembers the names already seen, and `unique` collects the rest.
A name that is not in the set yet is new: mark it and keep it.

slides.text:
A map can keep a **slice** under each key. To group values, append each one to the slice of its key. A missing key reads as a nil slice and `append` accepts one, so the first value needs no setup.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
for each word in words
    group[length of word] =
        group[length of word] plus word

slides.text: `append` returns the new slice and does not change the map. The result has to be stored back under the key, or the group stays as it was.

A value can also be another map: a map of maps. Reading through a missing outer key is safe, because it gives a nil inner map. **Writing** to a nil inner map stops the program, so make the inner map first when it is missing.

exercises.title: Group by a key
exercises.guide: Put each word in the group of its length.

chunks.guide: A list of words to group by length.
Each group is a slice stored under its length. A new length starts from a nil slice, and `append` accepts it.

notes.text: Stores the grown slice back under its key.

chunks.guide: Words keep the order they came in. A length nobody has gives a nil slice.

exercises.title: Even and odd groups
exercises.guide: Group the numbers by whether they are even. Print the even group and how many are odd.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `append` returns a new slice, and nothing stores it in `groups`. The map still holds `[1]` and has no `b`. Only the local `grown` and `fresh` grew.

exercises.title: A map of maps
exercises.guide: Keep the grades of each student, by subject.

chunks.guide: A map whose values are maps: each student has their own subjects.

notes.text: Each value is itself a map.

chunks.guide: A student with no inner map yet gets one before any write. Writing to a nil map stops the program.

notes.text: A missing student reads as a nil map.
The first index finds the inner map, the second its entry.

chunks.guide: Or build the whole inner map at once with a literal.
Reading through a missing student is safe: it gives 0 and adds nothing.

notes.text: A missing outer key still reads as 0.

exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick what it is for.
